learn: Some information in a text is explicit: the author states it directly.
An inference is a conclusion you reach by combining clues in the text with what you already know. If a character's umbrella drips as she walks in, you can infer it's raining.
Good readers make inferences and support them with evidence from the text.
check: A conclusion from clues plus what you know
A sentence copied word for word
A dripping umbrella lets you infer that...
lessons.try: Read a page of a story and write one inference with the clue that supports it.

learn: When you use evidence, you can quote the author's exact words inside quotation marks.
Introduce quotes with phrases like "The text states..." or "According to the author...".
Then explain how the quote supports your idea.
check: Explain how it supports your idea
lessons.try: Choose a quote from your book that shows a character's feelings and explain it.

learn: Annotating means marking a text as you read: underlining key ideas, circling new words and writing notes in the margins.
Symbols can help: ? for confusing parts, ! for surprises, * for important ideas.
Annotations make it easier to find evidence later.
check: Marking a text as you read
lessons.try: Annotate a short article using at least three different symbols.

learn: The theme is the message or life lesson of a story. It is usually not stated directly.
Themes are big ideas like "friendship takes effort" or "honesty is important".
To find a theme, ask: What did the main character learn? What does the author want readers to understand?
check: The message or life lesson of a story
Which question helps find a theme?
What did the main character learn?
lessons.try: Name the theme of a story you've read recently and explain how you know.

learn: A topic is a word or phrase, like "courage". A theme is a full sentence about the topic, like "Courage means acting even when you're afraid".
Different stories can share a topic but have different themes.
State themes as complete sentences.
check: Courage means acting even when afraid
Can stories share a topic but have different themes?
lessons.try: Turn the topic "kindness" into a theme statement.

learn: A fiction summary tells who, wants, but, so, then: Somebody wanted something, but there was a problem, so they did something, then it ended a certain way.
Keep it short and in your own words.
Leave out minor details and your opinions.
check: In "Somebody Wanted But So Then", "But" is the...
A summary should include your opinion.
Short and in your own words
lessons.try: Use "Somebody, Wanted, But, So, Then" to summarise a fairy tale.

learn: Authors reveal characters through their words, thoughts, actions, appearance and how others react to them.
Characters can be round (complex, with many traits) or flat (simple).
A dynamic character changes during the story; a static character stays the same.
check: A complex character with many traits is...
lessons.try: Describe a main character's thoughts, words and actions in one chart.

learn: Setting includes the place, time and mood.
A setting can create problems: a blizzard might trap characters.
Changing the setting would change the story.
lessons.try: Imagine your favourite story in a different setting. How would it change?

learn: Plot follows a pattern: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution.
The exposition introduces characters and setting. Rising action builds tension. The climax is the turning point.
Falling action and resolution show what happens after the climax.
check: The turning point of a story is the...
lessons.try: Draw a plot diagram for a story and label each part.

learn: Poems are written in lines and stanzas (groups of lines).
Many poems use rhythm (a beat) and rhyme (matching end sounds).
Free verse poems don't follow a set rhyme or rhythm.
check: A group of lines in a poem is a...
A poem without set rhyme or rhythm is...
lessons.try: Read Robert Louis Stevenson's "My Shadow" (1885) and count its stanzas.

learn: Plays are written to be performed. They have a cast of characters, dialogue and stage directions.
Stage directions, often in italics or brackets, tell actors how to move and speak.
Plays are divided into acts and scenes.
check: What tells actors how to move?
The list of characters is the...
lessons.try: Write a short scene with two characters and stage directions.

learn: Stories use paragraphs and chapters. Poems use lines and stanzas. Plays use dialogue and scenes.
The same story could be told in any of these forms.
Each form has strengths: poems are compact and musical; plays are meant to be seen.
check: Which is written to be performed?
Can the same story be told in different forms?
lessons.try: Rewrite a short fable as a short poem.

learn: In first-person point of view, the narrator is a character in the story and uses "I" and "me".
Readers only know what the narrator thinks and sees.
First person can feel personal and close.
lessons.try: Rewrite a paragraph from a story in first person.

learn: In third person, the narrator is outside the story and uses "he", "she" and "they".
Third-person limited follows one character's thoughts. Third-person omniscient knows all characters' thoughts.
Omniscient means "all-knowing".
lessons.try: Identify the point of view in three books on your shelf.

learn: The same event can look very different from two points of view.
A firsthand account is told by someone who was there. A secondhand account is told by someone who wasn't.
Comparing accounts helps you understand events more fully.
check: A firsthand account is told by...
A news article about something the reporter didn't see is...
lessons.try: Compare a diary entry about an event with a news article about the same event.

units.t: Main Idea and Text Structure in Nonfiction

learn: Longer texts have a main idea for the whole piece and main ideas for each section.
Headings often hint at section main ideas.
Combine section ideas to find the overall main idea.
check: Do longer texts have more than one main idea?
Yes, one per section plus overall
lessons.try: List the main idea of each section of an article, then the overall main idea.

learn: Chronological structure tells events in time order.
Compare and contrast shows similarities and differences. Cause and effect explains why things happen.
Problem and solution presents a problem and ways to solve it.
check: "Because of the drought, crops failed" shows...
Which structure presents a problem and ways to fix it?
lessons.try: Find an example of each structure in a science or history book.

learn: Charts, graphs, diagrams and timelines give information visually.
Read titles, labels and keys carefully.
Explain how a visual adds to the text.
check: What should you read carefully on a chart?
lessons.try: Find a diagram in a nonfiction book and explain what it adds.

learn: Many English words come from Greek and Latin roots.
"Tele" means far (telephone, television). "Graph" means write (autograph). "Port" means carry (transport).
"Bio" means life (biology). "Aud" means hear (audience).
lessons.try: List three words with each root: tele, port, bio.

learn: Definition clues give the meaning directly: "A herbivore, an animal that eats only plants, ..."
Synonym and antonym clues give similar or opposite words.
Example clues list examples of the word.
check: "A herbivore, an animal that eats only plants" is a...
An antonym clue gives a word that means...
lessons.try: Find a new word in your reading and name the kind of context clue that helps.

learn: A dictionary gives definitions, pronunciation and parts of speech.
A thesaurus gives synonyms and antonyms.
A glossary defines words used in one book.
check: A glossary defines words used in...
lessons.try: Look up one word in a dictionary and a thesaurus. Compare.

learn: A simile compares two things using "like" or "as": "Her smile was as bright as the sun."
A metaphor compares without those words: "The classroom was a zoo."
Both help readers picture ideas in fresh ways.
check: "As bright as the sun" is a...
"The classroom was a zoo" is a...
lessons.try: Write two similes and two metaphors about the weather.

learn: Personification gives human qualities to non-human things: "The wind whispered."
Hyperbole is extreme exaggeration: "I've told you a million times!"
Writers use these for effect and humour.
check: "I've told you a million times" is...
lessons.try: Write a sentence with personification about your house.

learn: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning differs from its words: "It's raining cats and dogs" means it's raining hard.
An adage or proverb is a well-known saying with advice: "Don't count your chickens before they hatch."
Context helps you understand idioms.
check: "Don't count your chickens before they hatch" is a...
lessons.try: Ask family members for their favourite idioms and what they mean.

learn: Relative pronouns (who, whose, whom, which, that) connect details: "The girl who won is my friend."
Progressive verbs show ongoing action: I am walking, I was walking, I will be walking.
Use "who" for people and "which" or "that" for things.
lessons.try: Write three sentences using who, which and that.

learn: Modal verbs show possibility or necessity: can, may, must, should, might.
Prepositional phrases begin with a preposition and show relationships: under the bridge, after lunch.
These add precise meaning.
lessons.try: Write a sentence with a modal verb and a prepositional phrase.

learn: Their (belonging), there (place) and they're (they are) are often confused.
To, too and two are also confused: to the store, too hot, two cats.
Use a comma before "and", "but" or "so" when joining two complete sentences.
check: Use a comma before "but" when it joins...
lessons.try: Write sentences using their, there and they're correctly.

units.t: The Writing Process and Types of Writing

learn: The writing process has five steps: prewriting, drafting, revising, editing and publishing.
Prewriting includes brainstorming and planning. Drafting is getting ideas down.
Revising improves ideas and organisation; editing fixes conventions.
lessons.try: Take a piece through all five steps.

learn: Opinion writing states a point of view, supports it with reasons and evidence, and ends with a conclusion.
Informative writing explains a topic with facts, definitions and details, grouped logically.
Both use transitions like "for instance", "in addition" and "consequently".
lessons.try: Write an informative paragraph about an animal with a heading and three facts.

learn: A narrative develops real or imagined experiences with descriptive details and clear event order.
Use dialogue and description to show characters' responses.
Use sensory details and a satisfying conclusion.
lessons.try: Write a one-page narrative about a time you felt proud.
